title: Tek-ko-kui, the Bamboo Giant
summary: A giant nature spirit made of bamboo who protects the forests of Taiwan from those who would harm them.
full_text:
In the misty mountains of Taiwan, where the bamboo grows so thick that sunlight barely reaches the forest floor, there lives a guardian of incredible age. The Tek-ko-kui is a giant whose body is made of jointed bamboo, his limbs creaking when he moves, his voice the sound of wind through hollow reeds. He stands taller than the tallest tree, and when he walks, the ground trembles.

The Tek-ko-kui is a spirit of the old forests, a remnant of the time before humans came to Taiwan. He watches over the bamboo groves, the stands of camphor, the hidden waterfalls. He is patient and slow, like the forest itself. He does not anger easily. But when loggers came with their iron saws and their trucks, the Tek-ko-kui stirred. Trees that were marked for cutting would be found split in half by morning. Saws would break for no reason. Loggers would lose their way in familiar woods.

An old Hakxa woman who lived at the edge of the forest knew how to speak to the Tek-ko-kui. She left offerings of rice wine and sticky rice at the base of the largest bamboo. In return, the giant protected her village from landslides and floods. When developers came to build a resort, she warned them. They laughed. Their bulldozers broke down one by one. Their surveyors reported seeing a giant figure watching from the treeline. The project was abandoned.

The Tek-ko-kui is still there, in the mountains of Taiwan, standing silent among the bamboo. He does not hate humans. He simply asks that the forest be respected. And those who listen to the wind in the bamboo can sometimes hear him breathing.
moral: The forest has its own protectors; take only what you need.

title: Mô-sîn-á, the Grass Spirit
summary: A mischievous grass spirit from Taiwanese Hokkien folklore who tangles the feet of travelers and leads them astray.
full_text:
The fields of Taiwan, especially in the countryside of the western plains, are home to a small but persistent spirit called Mô-sîn-á. Its name means 'grass spirit' or 'grass demon,' and it lives among the tall grasses that line the paths between rice paddies. Mô-sîn-á is a trickster, not a killer. Its favorite game is tangling the feet of travelers, tripping them at just the wrong moment.

Farmers know Mô-sîn-á well. A man walking home after a long day in the fields might suddenly find his feet caught in grass that seems to have grown around his ankles. He stumbles, falls, and when he looks back, the grass is perfectly normal. That is Mô-sîn-á at work. It is not malicious, merely playful, but its games can have serious consequences. A fall can break a hip or twist an ankle. A traveler delayed by Mô-sîn-á might find himself caught in a sudden rainstorm or arriving home after dark.

The best defense against Mô-sîn-á is to carry a small talisman, a piece of red cloth tied around the ankle, or to walk with a companion. The spirit prefers to target lone travelers. But the most effective protection is simply to acknowledge it. A farmer who stops and says, 'I know you are there, Mô-sîn-á. Let me pass, and I will leave a pinch of rice for you,' will find his feet free. The fields of Taiwan are vast, and the paths are many. But walk with respect, and Mô-sîn-á will let you pass.
moral: Acknowledgment and respect disarm even the most playful spirits.

title: Hóu-koô-pô, the Tiger Spirit
summary: A protective tiger spirit who guards the mountains of Taiwan, appearing to those who are lost or in danger.
full_text:
In the mountains of eastern Taiwan, where the cloud forests give way to sheer cliffs and deep gorges, the indigenous tribes tell stories of Hóu-koô-pô. This is no ordinary tiger, but a spirit in the form of a great striped cat, larger than any living tiger, with eyes that glow like amber lanterns in the dark. Hóu-koô-pô is a protector, not a predator. It guards the mountain paths and watches over those who travel with good intentions.

Hunters who respect the old ways, who pray before the hunt and waste nothing, may catch a glimpse of Hóu-koô-pô watching from a ridge. Its presence is a blessing: a promise of safe passage and good fortune. But those who hunt for sport, who kill without need, will find Hóu-koô-pô blocking their path, a silent wall of muscle and fury. It does not attack. It does not need to. The mere sight of it is enough to drive a man to his knees in terror.

A hunter from Hualien once boasted that he would bring back a tiger skin, not knowing that the last real tiger in Taiwan had been killed decades earlier. He was guided by an old man who knew the mountains. On the third night, they saw a pair of golden eyes in the darkness. The hunter raised his rifle. The old man knocked it aside. 'That is Hóu-koô-pô,' he whispered. 'You cannot kill a spirit.' The hunter fled the mountain that night. He never hunted again.

Hóu-koô-pô is still there, in the high forests of Taiwan. When you hear a sound in the darkness that is too large to be a deer and too deliberate to be the wind, you are hearing Hóu-koô-pô. Stand still. Bow your head. And walk on.
moral: Some guardians cannot be defeated, only respected.
